script.opening: (Polite, a little exasperated; touches her chest and ear.) "Thanks for seeing me. I've got these lumpy scars — this one on my chest started from a spot, and the one on my ear from a piercing. They're itchy and they've got bigger than the original mark. I had the chest one cut out before and it came back worse and bigger. I've got my sister's wedding in a few months — can you just cut it off properly this time?"

facts.text: Chest: started from a spot about three years ago, kept growing; cut out at a private clinic 18 months ago, came back within months "wider than it was before they cut it" — now about 4 cm, raised, shiny, darker than her skin. Earlobe: from a piercing two years ago, now a firm lump "like a marble". Will show both on camera.
"They just itch, and the chest one's sometimes tender." Itch keeps her awake some nights. No bleeding, ulceration or discharge.
"I'm not sure. Nobody mentioned anything else" — no steroid injections, silicone or pressure after the excision as far as she knows.
"Not at the moment. Why?" Not pregnant, not breastfeeding; on the combined pill.
No other medical problems. Combined pill only. No allergies. Her mum has a keloid on her shoulder from a vaccination.
Pharmacy student. Lives with her parents. Non-smoker. The wedding is in four months; she will be a bridesmaid in a strapless dress.
If asked: "Everyone will see it in the photos. I'm so self-conscious about it, and the itching drives me mad." Wears high necklines. Her aunties comment on it.

Hopeful at first that a better surgeon will fix it: "I think they just didn't do it properly." If told honestly that cutting alone often makes it worse, go quiet: "(Quiet.) So I'm stuck with it." Brightens if offered realistic options and a timeline: "Would the injections work before the wedding?" If the doctor promises it can be cut out cleanly, accept eagerly (the trap).

ice.ideas: "The last surgeon didn't do it properly. Cut out properly, it'll be gone."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — being looked at in her sister's wedding photos and comments from family; the constant itch; worried it will keep getting bigger.
ice.expectations: "Cut it off properly this time, before the wedding."

cues: "It came back worse and bigger." — the key history; invites the honest conversation about excision.
"My sister's wedding in a few months." — the deadline and the emotional weight.
"So I'm stuck with it." — disappointment to respond to with empathy.

checkpoints.text: Recognises KELOID (growth beyond the wound margin, itch/tenderness, predilection in darker skin and at chest/earlobe/shoulder sites, recurrence) and distinguishes it from a hypertrophic scar (within wound margins, tends to regress)
Is HONEST that simple surgical excision alone has a high recurrence rate and can worsen/enlarge a keloid — directly addressing the "just cut it off" request rather than agreeing to it

Outlines realistic, control-focused options — intralesional corticosteroid (± cryotherapy), including its side effects (skin thinning, hypopigmentation more visible on darker skin), silicone gel/sheets, pressure devices (e.g. pressure earrings), and specialist excision only when combined with adjuvant steroid injection or pressure — and sets the expectation of control, not guaranteed cure, with common recurrence
Gives prevention advice for a keloid-prone individual (avoid non-essential trauma/piercings on prone sites, treat new lesions early, silicone/pressure after wounds) without blame
Refers appropriately (dermatology ± plastics for selected earlobe keloids with combined excision + adjuvant therapy) rather than attempting or promising simple removal
Handles the consultation with CULTURAL SENSITIVITY and takes the cosmetic/emotional impact (wedding, self-consciousness, itch) seriously — neither minimising nor being discouraging
Communicates the honest limits of treatment with empathy, acknowledges the previous recurrence, checks understanding, and supports realistic expectations

Safety-nets and follows up: a clear management/referral plan with realistic timeframe relative to the wedding, symptom relief (itch) in the meantime, what to expect from treatment and recurrence, and review — honesty and support, not an over-promised clean removal

worked.txt: "What you’ve got are keloid scars — scar tissue that overgrows beyond the original mark. They’re common in people with skin like yours and at spots like the chest and earlobes, and they can be itchy and uncomfortable, so I understand why they’re bothering you, especially with the wedding."

"Here’s the honest part, and it explains what happened last time: simply cutting a keloid out often makes it come back — sometimes bigger — because the new cut can keloid too. So ‘just cutting it off’ isn’t the reliable fix it sounds like, and I don’t want to set you up for the same disappointment."

"What does help is treatments aimed at flattening and softening them and easing the itch — steroid injections, sometimes with freezing, silicone gel or sheets, and pressure earrings for the ear one. I should be upfront that the injections can thin the skin and leave a paler patch, which shows more on darker skin, so that’s something to weigh up with the specialist. If surgery’s ever used, it has to be combined with these to stop it returning. The honest goal is good control, not a guaranteed clean cure — and they can recur."

"Because your skin is prone to this, it’s worth avoiding extra piercings or non-essential procedures on areas like the chest and ears, and treating any new lumpy scar early. That’s not you having done anything wrong — it’s just how your skin heals."

"I’m going to refer you to the skin specialists — and for the earlobe, possibly the plastic surgery team who do combined treatment. I’ll be honest that a few months may not fully flatten them before the wedding, but we can start treatment now to improve them and settle the itch."

"In the meantime I can help with the itch, and silicone gel is worth starting. If a scar suddenly changes a lot, becomes painful, ulcerates or bleeds, come back. We’ll go through the specialist plan together and keep your expectations realistic but hopeful."

f.learning: KELOID scarring is scar tissue that grows BEYOND the boundary of the original wound, often itchy or tender, with a strong predilection in people with darker skin (African, Caribbean, Asian heritage) and at sites such as the chest, shoulders, upper back, earlobes and jawline — distinguished from a HYPERTROPHIC scar, which stays within the wound margins and tends to regress. The central, examinable honesty is that simple surgical EXCISION ALONE has a high recurrence rate and can make a keloid worse/larger (because the fresh wound itself keloids), so the natural request to "just cut it off" must be addressed directly rather than agreed to; any surgery must be combined with adjuvant therapy (intralesional steroid, pressure, selected radiotherapy) under specialist care. Realistic options are control-focused: intralesional corticosteroid injections (± cryotherapy) to flatten/soften and reduce itch — with side effects of skin thinning and hypopigmentation that are more visible on darker skin — silicone gel/sheets, and pressure devices (e.g. pressure earrings), often combined with each other or with specialist excision (BAD keloids leaflet, 2017) — with the explicit expectation that the aim is control, not guaranteed cure, and that recurrence is common. Give prevention advice for a keloid-prone individual (avoid non-essential trauma/piercings on prone sites, treat new lesions early, silicone/pressure after wounds) without blame, and refer to dermatology (± plastics for selected earlobe keloids). Throughout, handle the consultation with cultural sensitivity — keloids disproportionately affect people with darker skin — and take the cosmetic and emotional impact (here, an upcoming wedding and self-consciousness) seriously, communicating honest limits with empathy rather than minimising or over-promising.

knowledge.guideline: BAD patient information leaflet: Keloids (updated October 2017) · BAD leaflet: Intralesional steroid therapy
knowledge.summary: A scar that grows beyond the original wound, itches and returned larger after excision is a keloid. Excision alone rarely succeeds; treatment aims for control with steroid injections, silicone and pressure, under specialist care.

points.t: A keloid spreads beyond the original area of skin damage and can follow very minor injury (BAD 2017). A hypertrophic scar stays within the wound and tends to flatten with time. Chest, shoulders, upper back and earlobes are typical keloid sites, and people with darker skin are more often affected.

BAD (2017): surgical excision is rarely successful because it makes a larger wound and the keloid is likely to regrow; compression dressings or steroid injections after excision may reduce the risk. Excision is a specialist decision, combined with adjuvant treatment.

Triamcinolone acetonide injected into the keloid can flatten it and ease itch, usually as a course of injections several weeks apart (dose per BNF). Side effects include skin thinning and lightening of skin colour — more visible on darker skin, so discuss it openly.
Silicone gel or sheets and pressure (for example pressure earrings after earlobe treatment) help flatten and soften scars and are used after treatment to reduce recurrence.
Avoid further piercings and non-essential cosmetic procedures, especially on the chest, shoulders and earlobes; treat acne and new keloids early. Frame this as a skin tendency, not a fault.
A lesion that bleeds, ulcerates, grows quickly or looks different from her other scars, or a ‘keloid’ with no history of skin injury, needs review for another diagnosis, including skin cancer.

Keloid vs hypertrophic scar; considered another diagnosis if a lesion bleeds, ulcerates or behaves differently.
Screened for bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth or atypical change needing review for skin cancer.
Named keloid clearly, explained why excision alone recurs, without blame.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

model.text: Hello Amara, I’m Dr Lee. It sounds like these scars have been a real nuisance, and you’ve already been through one operation that didn’t work. Tell me about them.
model.why: Acknowledges her experience and opens the story

model.text: The chest one started from a spot and just kept growing. The ear one’s from a piercing. They’re itchy and sometimes sore. I had the chest one cut out and it came back bigger. And my sister’s getting married in a few months.
Thank you. I’d like to understand them properly, then be honest with you about what works, and agree a plan that has the wedding in mind. Is that okay?
Yes, please.
Could you show me both on the camera? Did they grow beyond the size of the original spot and piercing?
model.why: Uses video to assess the defining feature of keloid

model.text: (Shows chest and ear.) Yes, way bigger. The chest one’s wider than it was before they cut it.
That’s helpful. Has either ever bled, broken down, grown very quickly, or changed colour differently from the rest?
model.why: Screens for features that suggest another diagnosis

model.text: No. They just itch, and the chest one’s sometimes tender.
Do you know what was done after the chest one was cut out — any injections or pressure dressings?
model.why: Establishes whether adjuvant therapy was used

model.text: I’m not sure. Nobody mentioned anything else.
Do you get spots on your chest or back at the moment, or are you planning any more piercings or procedures?
model.why: Looks for ongoing triggers and prevention opportunities

model.text: Not at the moment. Why?
What do you think went wrong last time?
I think they just didn’t do it properly. If a better surgeon cut it out, it’d be gone.
And how are the scars affecting you — especially with the wedding coming?
model.why: Explores the emotional and cultural impact

model.text: Everyone will see it in the photos. I’m so self-conscious about it, and the itching drives me mad.
That sounds really hard — wanting to enjoy your sister’s day and feeling the scar will be what people see. I want to help with that, honestly and properly.
model.why: Validates the distress without minimising it

model.text: These are keloid scars. They’re an overgrowth of scar tissue that spreads beyond the original wound. They’re more common in people with darker skin, and on the chest and earlobes. It’s the way your skin heals, not anything you did.
model.why: Names keloid, contrasts with ordinary scars, without blame

model.text: So can it be cut out?

I’ll be straight with you. Cutting a keloid out on its own usually doesn’t work — the cut makes a new, bigger wound, and that heals as keloid too. That’s probably what happened last time; it wasn’t just the surgeon.
model.why: Honest about excision failing, addressing her idea directly

model.text: (Quiet.) So I’m stuck with it.

No — there are treatments that help. Steroid injections into the scar can flatten it and calm the itch, usually a few sessions weeks apart. Silicone gel or sheets and pressure help too. Occasionally specialists do surgery, but always with injections or other treatment afterwards to stop it coming back. The aim is to control it, and it can come back, so we keep an eye on it.
Would the injections work before the wedding?

It may flatten and itch less within a few months, but I can’t promise it will be gone. The injections can also lighten the skin a bit, which shows more on darker skin — that’s something to weigh up with the dermatologist. Make-up or camouflage products can help for the day itself.
model.why: Realistic timescale and skin-of-colour side effect

model.text: What I suggest is a referral to dermatology for injections and a proper plan for both scars. Meanwhile, silicone gel on the chest scar may help the itch. And because your skin forms keloids, I’d advise against any more piercings or non-essential procedures in future — especially on the ears, chest and shoulders. Does that make sense?
model.why: Referral, interim relief and prevention advice

model.text: I didn’t know that. Yes, that makes sense.

If either scar bleeds, breaks down, grows very fast or starts to look different from the others, let me know quickly — that would need a different check. Otherwise I’ll send the referral today. Can you tell me the plan back in your words?
Don’t just cut it out. Injections at dermatology, silicone gel for now, no more piercings. And tell you if it changes.
That’s it exactly. I’ll also send you some information about keloids, and we’ll speak again once you’ve seen dermatology. Thank you, Amara.

social.t: A visible scar before a family wedding has real emotional weight. Ask what it means to her.
Keloids are more common in people of African heritage. Piercing and other cultural or fashion practices matter; advise without judging.

legal.t: GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020): she needs to know the realistic chance of benefit, the recurrence risk and side effects such as skin lightening before choosing a treatment.

professional.t: Explain why the previous excision recurred without criticising another clinician (GMC Good Medical Practice, 2024).
Describe signs and side effects as they appear on darker skin; do not assume textbook images apply.

community.t: BAD patient leaflets on keloids and intralesional steroid therapy; Changing Faces for support with visible difference.
Specialist camouflage make-up for the wedding day while treatment takes effect.

redFlags: Bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth or a lesion unlike her other scars → review for another diagnosis, including skin cancer
A ‘keloid’ with no preceding skin injury or unusual site → reconsider the diagnosis
Any further piercing or cosmetic procedure → high risk of new keloid
psychosocial: Frustration and loss of trust after the failed excision
Itch and tenderness affecting clothing and daily comfort
ice: Idea: the previous surgeon didn’t do it properly
Concern: the scar will be seen at the wedding; itch and discomfort
Expectation: to have it cut off before the wedding

playbook.diagnosis: “These are keloid scars — scar tissue that keeps growing beyond the original wound. It’s the way your skin heals, and it’s more common with darker skin.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your skin’s repair system doesn’t know when to stop, so it keeps laying down scar tissue past the edge of the wound. Cutting it out gives it a new wound to overgrow — so we calm it down instead.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted it cut out before the wedding, and I understand why. I’d rather give you something that helps than something that may make it bigger again.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around the wedding with a realistic timescale, camouflage for the day, and no blame for her skin type.
sharedPlan: Dermatology referral for intralesional triamcinolone (course of injections; dose per BNF), with silicone and pressure
Silicone gel or sheets for the chest scar now for itch and softening
Avoid new piercings and non-essential procedures; treat new keloids early
safetyNet: Bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth or change → review promptly
Warn about skin thinning and lightening with injections; review after the dermatology plan

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by saying yes to the request. The marks go to an honest ‘no, but here’s what helps’, delivered with warmth.

items.fail: Referring for simple excision because she asked.
items.why: BAD (2017): excision is rarely successful and the keloid is likely to regrow, often larger.
items.fix: Explain why, then offer the treatments that control it.

items.fail: Not distinguishing keloid from hypertrophic scar.
items.why: Hypertrophic scars settle; keloids spread beyond the wound and recur. The distinction drives the advice.
items.fix: Ask whether it grew beyond the original wound, and look on camera.

items.fail: Blaming the previous surgeon, or her.
items.why: Criticism of colleagues or implied fault damages trust and professionalism.
items.fix: “It’s how keloids behave — cutting alone makes a new wound for them to grow into.”

items.fail: Promising injections will make it vanish before the wedding.
items.why: Over-promising leads to disappointment; response takes months and recurrence is common.
items.fix: Say it may flatten and itch less, name skin lightening, and offer camouflage for the day.

items.why: Prevention is part of the task; a new piercing in a keloid-prone person is a predictable harm.
items.fix: Ask about future piercings or procedures and advise against non-essential ones.

items.why: Ignores the emotional and cultural weight of a visible scar at a family wedding.
items.fix: Ask what the wedding means to her and plan with it in mind.

timeMap.d: She has been let down once. Acknowledge the failed excision and the wedding early.
Show both on camera: beyond the wound? Itch, tenderness, bleeding, ulceration, rapid change. What happened after the excision. Future piercings.
Her idea (bad surgery) and the wedding photos. Validate the distress.
Keloid; why excision alone recurs; injections, silicone, pressure; control not cure; skin lightening on darker skin.
Dermatology referral; silicone now; no new piercing; camouflage for the day; changes to report; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees to refer for simple excision; or says nothing can be done; doesn’t explain keloid; ignores the wedding and her distress.
wordPics.pass: Recognises keloid; explains excision alone often recurs; offers dermatology for steroid injections with silicone and pressure; sets expectation of control; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores what the wedding means to her; addresses her belief that the surgeon was at fault kindly; discusses skin lightening from injections on darker skin; gives prevention advice on future piercings; offers practical help for the day; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “I’ll refer you to have it cut out properly.”
avoid.instead: “Cutting it out on its own usually makes it come back bigger. Let’s get you the treatment that controls it.”
avoid.why: Agreeing to simple excision is the clinical fail in this station.

avoid.dont: “There’s nothing we can do about keloids.”
avoid.instead: “There are treatments that flatten them and ease the itch — the aim is control.”
avoid.why: Nihilism is as wrong as over-promising, and loses her trust.

avoid.instead: “It clearly matters to you, especially with the wedding. Let’s plan with that in mind.”
avoid.why: Minimising a visible difference loses Relating marks.

social.t: A visible scar before a family wedding has real emotional weight. Ask what it means to her.
Keloids are more common in people of African heritage. Piercing and other cultural or fashion practices matter; advise without judging.

legal.t: GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020): she needs to know the realistic chance of benefit, the recurrence risk and side effects such as skin lightening before choosing a treatment.

professional.t: Explain why the previous excision recurred without criticising another clinician (GMC Good Medical Practice, 2024).
Describe signs and side effects as they appear on darker skin; do not assume textbook images apply.

community.t: BAD patient leaflets on keloids and intralesional steroid therapy; Changing Faces for support with visible difference.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “These are keloid scars — scar tissue that keeps growing beyond the original wound. It’s the way your skin heals, and it’s more common with darker skin.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your skin’s repair system doesn’t know when to stop, so it keeps laying down scar tissue past the edge of the wound. Cutting it out gives it a new wound to overgrow — so we calm it down instead.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted it cut out before the wedding, and I understand why. I’d rather give you something that helps than something that may make it bigger again.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around the wedding with a realistic timescale, camouflage for the day, and no blame for her skin type.

Avoid new piercings and non-essential procedures; treat new keloids early

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by saying yes to the request. The marks go to an honest ‘no, but here’s what helps’, delivered with warmth.

items.fail: Referring for simple excision because she asked.
items.why: BAD (2017): excision is rarely successful and the keloid is likely to regrow, often larger.
items.fix: Explain why, then offer the treatments that control it.

items.fail: Not distinguishing keloid from hypertrophic scar.
items.why: Hypertrophic scars settle; keloids spread beyond the wound and recur. The distinction drives the advice.
items.fix: Ask whether it grew beyond the original wound, and look on camera.

items.fail: Blaming the previous surgeon, or her.
items.why: Criticism of colleagues or implied fault damages trust and professionalism.
items.fix: “It’s how keloids behave — cutting alone makes a new wound for them to grow into.”

items.fail: Promising injections will make it vanish before the wedding.
items.why: Over-promising leads to disappointment; response takes months and recurrence is common.
items.fix: Say it may flatten and itch less, name skin lightening, and offer camouflage for the day.

items.why: Prevention is part of the task; a new piercing in a keloid-prone person is a predictable harm.
items.fix: Ask about future piercings or procedures and advise against non-essential ones.

items.why: Ignores the emotional and cultural weight of a visible scar at a family wedding.
items.fix: Ask what the wedding means to her and plan with it in mind.
